ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.problem: UAV autopilots accept MAVLink traffic over a network link. If the parser mishandles malformed, truncated or length-inconsistent frames, the communication endpoint becomes a failure point for the whole airborne node. Robustness of that endpoint had not been characterised for the MAVLink 2 ArduCopter SITL build in use.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.objective: Build a reproducible protocol-level fuzzing framework for ArduCopter Software-In-The-Loop and characterise how it behaves under random, boundary-value and structurally malformed MAVLink 2 input, with every run logged as evidence.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.approach: Adapt the seven-case fuzzing methodology published by Domin, Symeonidis and Marin (2016) from MAVLink 1 to MAVLink 2. The original work targeted MAVLink 1 frames (magic byte FE); this is an independent reimplementation for the MAVLink 2 wire format (FD), its 3-byte message ID and its one-byte payload-length field, with CRC-extra values taken from the installed pymavlink message map.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.architecture: A Windows fuzzing host drives the ArduCopter SITL MAVLink/TCP endpoint on port 5760. A separate monitor service on the SITL host reports, over TCP port 9001, whether the arducopter process is alive and whether 5760 is still listening — so a fault is detected independently of the fuzzer's own socket.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.implementation: Built a controlled security-testing environment using ArduPilot/ArduCopter SITL on Ubuntu and a Python-based fuzzing client on Windows. The system communicates with ArduCopter over TCP port 5760, while a separate Ubuntu SITL monitor tracks the ArduCopter process and the listening state of the SITL port. Original study: MAVLink 1 methodology. This implementation: MAVLink 2 adaptation — the packet layer was rewritten for the MAVLink 2 frame format (FD), its 3-byte message ID and its one-byte payload-length field, with CRC-extra values taken from the installed pymavlink message map.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.results: Cases 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 completed with no crash detected. Case 2 did not complete its full 65,280-test matrix and its corrected rerun is outstanding. No vulnerability was discovered, and no claim of correctness or security is made on the basis of these runs.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.title: MAVLink 2 Security Testing — ArduCopter SITL Fuzzing
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.summary: Designed and implemented a Python-based MAVLink 2 fuzzing framework for ArduCopter Software-In-The-Loop (SITL), adapting the fuzzing methodology described in a published 2016 MAVLink security study to a modern MAVLink 2 environment. The project includes reproducible test generation, TCP-based protocol fuzzing, automated SITL monitoring, human-readable test logging, and seven structured fuzzing cases.

ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.testNote: No crash detected during the completed test campaigns. That means the monitor observed no ArduCopter process termination and no loss of the listening socket at the time of each check — it is not a finding that the parser is free of defects, and no vulnerability is claimed.
ices-mavlink2-arducopter-sitl-fuzzing.reference: This project adapts the fuzzing methodology described by Domin, Symeonidis, and Marin (2016) from a MAVLink 1 environment to a modern MAVLink 2 / ArduCopter SITL environment. Karel Domin, Iraklis Symeonidis and Eduard Marin, “Security Analysis of the Drone Communication Protocol: Fuzzing the MAVLink Protocol”, 2016. The paper is the methodological reference and the work of its own authors; this repository is an independent implementation and is not their work.
